text: . Pleural effusions. Talc is used as a sclerosant to achieve pleu- rodesis in the management of benign and malignant pleural effu- sions (p.659) and recurrent spontaneous pneumothorax.1-4 It is generally given into the pleural space as a slurry via intercostal tube, or by insufflation (talc poudrage) at thoracoscopy. Most re- ports have used a dose of 2 to 5 g, but doses have ranged from 1 to 10 g. A study5 of talc pleurodesis in patients with malignant pleural effusion found both slurry and insufflation to be equally effective. The most common adverse effects associated with this use of talc are pain and fever. Other reported effects have includ- ed local infection and empyema, cardiovascular complications, and respiratory failure (see also Effects on the Lungs, above). 1. Kennedy L, Sahn SA. Talc pleurodesis for the treatment of pneu- mothorax and pleural effusion. Chest 1994; 106: 1215–22. 2. de Campos JRM, et al. Thoracoscopy talc poudrage: a 15 year experience.
